**Conversation Overview**

The person is a course creator and educator at The Luxora Collective (theluxoracollective.co), building out a comprehensive training curriculum for independent med spa owners. The conversation focused on developing new course playbook modules in a specific branded Word document format that matches previously established Luxora styling: formal language without contractions, no em dashes, ranges written as "x to y," no page breaks, 11pt Arial body text, mauve and plum brand palette, and consistent header and footer treatments with page numbers.

Three complete playbook modules were built during this conversation. The first was a Med Spa SOP Playbook covering sixteen industry-standard operating procedures across four categories: client experience and front of house, clinical and compliance, revenue and growth, and operations and team. Each SOP included purpose, when it runs, a ready-to-use procedure, implementation guidance, and team training instructions, along with a standard SOP anatomy template, a seven-step method for writing any procedure from scratch, a rollout and training method, and a four-phase eight-week implementation roadmap with a master SOP index. After delivering the SOP playbook, the person asked for a strategic recommendation on what additional playbooks would most benefit their students. Claude identified that the existing library was strong on revenue generation but thin on cost-side management, and recommended a prioritized list led by a Profit and Numbers Playbook and a Compensation and Incentive Playbook, with Retail as a Profit Center, Capacity and Scheduling, Acquisition Economics, and an Annual Promotional Calendar also named. Here is the new course module, built as a complete playbook your students can use immediately.

**What is inside (12 pages, four parts):**

Part One teaches the skill itself, so owners are not dependent on you to write the next procedure. It covers what an SOP is and why it matters more in a med spa than almost anywhere else, the standard format every procedure should follow (a fillable anatomy template), a seven step method to write any SOP from scratch, a roll out and training method, and a maintenance cadence.

Part Two is the library: sixteen industry standard SOPs across four categories. Each one gives Purpose, When it runs, a ready to use Procedure, How to implement, and How to train the team.
- Client Experience: Inbound Inquiry and Speed to Lead, New Client Intake and Consultation, Check Out and Rebooking, Reminders and No Shows.
- Clinical, Compliance, and Safety: Treatment Protocol and Pre and Post Care, Sanitation and Room Turnover, Consent and Privacy, Adverse Event and Emergency Response.
- Revenue: Consultation to Treatment Plan Conversion (cross referenced to the Conversion Playbook), Membership and Package Enrollment, Review Generation, Lead Follow Up and Reactivation.
- Operations and Team: Daily Opening and Closing, Payment and Reconciliation, Inventory and Retail, New Team Member Onboarding.

Part Three is an eight week implementation roadmap so owners install in the right order, safety first, then experience, then revenue, then operations depth.

Part Four is a Master SOP Index pre filled with all sixteen procedures, ready for owners to add owner names and review dates.

Brand rules are all honored: no em dashes, formal full words throughout, ranges written as "x to y," no page breaks, no consultant jargon.

**The two weakest parts, as always:**

1. **The clinical SOPs lean generic on purpose, and that is a real limitation.** Treatment Protocol, Adverse Event, and Consent are the procedures where state board rules, scope of practice, and medical director requirements vary the most, so I kept them at a safe framework level with caution notes. If this course serves a defined market, the module would be stronger with a short "how to localize the clinical four to your state" worksheet, otherwise a few owners may treat the templates as complete when they are starting points.

2. **Sixteen SOPs in one module risks overwhelm, which is the exact problem the roadmap warns against.** The roadmap softens it, but a student could still feel they need all sixteen before they open their doors. Consider whether to split this into a "core six to launch" lead module and an "expand to sixteen" follow up, so the entry point feels lighter and the rest becomes an upsell or later lesson.
